did_you_know.text: Did you know? Habakkuk describes himself as a watchman standing at his post and waiting for the Lord’s answer to his complaint. Thus the chapter opens with the image of a prophet who listens and waits for a response.
Did you know? The Lord commands Habakkuk to write down the vision and make it clear on tablets, so that the reader may understand it and run with its message.
Did you know? The vision is tied to an appointed time. Even if it seems to be delayed, the prophet is told to wait for it, because it will surely come and will not be late.

Did you know? The verse contrasts the person whose desires are not right with the righteous, of whom it says, “But the righteous will live by his faithfulness.” This is one of the chapter’s central verses.

Did you know? The conqueror is portrayed as arrogant and never satisfied, expanding his desire like Sheol and gathering many nations to himself. Yet his power and appetite do not bring him satisfaction.

Did you know? The nations will take up a taunt, a proverb, and riddles against the conqueror. In this way, the chapter describes how the oppressed will turn his downfall into a subject of ridicule and condemnation.
Did you know? The reason for the conqueror’s downfall is stated explicitly: he plundered many nations and acted through human bloodshed and violence against the land, the city, and its inhabitants.

Did you know? Even the building materials are portrayed as witnesses to injustice: the stone from the wall cries out, and the wooden beam answers it. The image emphasizes that the violence cannot be hidden.

Did you know? In contrast to the nations’ violent toil, the chapter presents a sweeping vision: the whole earth will be filled with the knowledge of the glory of the Lord, as the waters cover the sea.
Did you know? At the end of the chapter, the silent idols are contrasted with the Lord in his holy temple. Therefore, the final command is: “Let all the earth be silent before him.”
